content: ADAR, or adenosine deaminase acting on RNA, is an enzyme encoded by the ADAR gene in humans. This enzyme specifically binds to double-stranded RNA (dsRNA) and catalyzes the conversion of adenosine (A) to inosine (I) through a process called deamination. ADAR proteins are RNA-binding proteins that play a critical role in RNA editing by modifying the nucleotide content of RNA transcripts after transcription. This A-to-I conversion disrupts the normal adenosine-uridine (A:U) base pairing, rendering the RNA molecule less stable. Inosine structurally resembles guanine (G), which allows it to pair with cytosine (C) and mimic guanosine during translation. This editing process can lead to codon changes, potentially altering the coding sequences of proteins and their functions. However, most editing events occur in noncoding regions of RNA, such as untranslated regions (UTRs), Alu elements, and long interspersed nuclear elements (LINEs). Mutations in the ADAR gene have been linked to diseases such as dyschromatosis symmetrica hereditaria and Aicardi–Goutières syndrome. Additionally, alternative splicing of the ADAR gene produces different isoforms, which have been characterized. Beyond its editing functions, ADAR also influences the transcriptome in editing-independent ways, likely by interacting with other RNA-binding proteins. Discovery ADAR and its gene were first discovered in 1987 by Brenda Bass and Harold Weintraub during their research on Xenopus laevis embryos. They were investigating gene function using antisense RNA inhibition but encountered unexpected results when applying their protocols to embryos. Their subsequent studies revealed a developmentally regulated activity that denatures RNA:RNA hybrids in embryos. In 1988, Richard Wagner and colleagues further characterized this activity, identifying a protein responsible for unwinding dsRNA. This protein was found to specifically target dsRNA without requiring ATP and modified the RNA beyond the point of rehybridization through adenosine deamination to inosine. This modification caused mismatched base pairing between inosine and uridine, destabilizing and unwinding the dsRNA. Function and Evolution ADAR-mediated RNA editing is one of the most common forms of RNA modification and exhibits both selective and non-selective activity. By converting adenosine to inosine, ADAR can regulate gene expression and modify the functionality of small RNA molecules. It is believed that ADAR evolved from ADAT (adenosine deaminase acting on tRNA), a protein essential in all eukaryotes, during the early metazoan period. This evolutionary process likely involved the addition of a dsRNA-binding domain to a duplicated ADAT gene. The ADAR gene family has been highly conserved throughout evolution, underscoring its importance as a regulatory mechanism in metazoan organisms. Notably, ADAR has not been identified in non-metazoan eukaryotes such as plants, fungi, and choanoflagellates. Types of ADAR In mammals, there are three types of ADAR enzymes: ADAR1, ADAR2, and ADAR3. ADAR1 and ADAR2 are catalytically active and expressed in various tissues, while ADAR3 is found exclusively in the brain and is thought to be catalytically inactive. ADAR1 exists in two isoforms, ADAR1p150 and ADAR1p110. ADAR1p110 is localized to the nucleus, whereas ADAR1p150 shuttles between the nucleus and cytoplasm. Despite sharing functional domains and expression patterns, ADAR1 and ADAR2 differ in their RNA editing activities. Catalytic Activity ADAR enzymes catalyze the hydrolytic deamination of adenosine to inosine using an activated water molecule for nucleophilic attack. This reaction involves the addition of water to carbon 6 of adenosine and the removal of ammonia, forming a hydrated intermediate. The active site of ADAR enzymes contains 2-3 N-terminal dsRNA-binding domains (dsRBDs) and a C-terminal catalytic deaminase domain. The dsRBDs feature a conserved α-β-β-β-α configuration. ADAR1 also has two Z-DNA-binding domains, Zα and Zβ, while ADAR2 and ADAR3 possess an arginine-rich single-stranded RNA (ssRNA)-binding domain. The catalytic core includes residues such as glutamic acid (E396), histidine (H394), and cysteines (C451 and C516) that coordinate a zinc ion, which activates the water molecule for hydrolytic deamination. Additionally, inositol hexakisphosphate (IP6) stabilizes arginine and lysine residues within the catalytic core. Dimerization In mammals, ADAR1 and ADAR2 require homodimerization for A-to-I editing, whereas ADAR3 does not. Studies have shown that dimerization can occur independently of RNA binding, suggesting that protein-protein interactions drive this process. Model Organisms Model organisms, such as conditional knockout mice, have been used to study ADAR function. For example, a mouse line with a targeted deletion of the ADAR gene revealed that homozygous mutant embryos rarely survive gestation, and none survive to weaning. Heterozygous mutant adult mice, however, exhibit no significant abnormalities. Role in Disease Aicardi–Goutières Syndrome Mutations in ADAR1 are associated with Aicardi–Goutières syndrome, a genetic inflammatory disorder affecting the skin and brain. Loss of ADAR1 function prevents the destabilization of dsRNA, which the immune system misinterprets as viral RNA, triggering an autoimmune response. HIV ADAR1 has a dual role in HIV infection. Elevated ADAR1 expression during infection can introduce A-to-G mutations in the HIV genome, inhibiting viral replication. However, these mutations may also lead to beneficial viral adaptations, such as drug resistance. Hepatocellular Carcinoma In hepatocellular carcinoma (HCC), ADAR1 is frequently upregulated, while ADAR2 is downregulated. This imbalance disrupts normal A-to-I editing patterns, with ADAR1 acting as an oncogene and ADAR2 functioning as a tumor suppressor. Dysregulated ADAR expression may serve as a prognostic marker for poor outcomes in HCC. Melanoma In contrast to HCC, loss of ADAR1 contributes to melanoma progression and metastasis. ADAR1 influences microRNA (miRNA) biogenesis, stability, and target binding. For example, downregulation of ADAR1 by CREB (cAMP-response element-binding protein) limits its ability to edit miRNAs like miR-455-5p. The unedited miR-455-5p downregulates the tumor suppressor protein CPEB1, promoting melanoma progression. Dyschromatosis Symmetrica Hereditaria (DSH1) Mutations in ADAR1, such as Gly1007Arg, have been implicated in DSH1, a disorder characterized by hyperpigmentation of the hands and feet, observed in some Japanese and Chinese families. Viral Activity Antiviral ADAR1 is an interferon-inducible protein that contributes to the immune response against pathogens. It has been shown to inhibit replication of viruses such as HCV, lymphocytic choriomeningitis virus (LCMV), and polyomavirus. Proviral In other contexts, ADAR1 can enhance viral replication. For example, in measles virus (MV), ADAR1 promotes replication through RNA editing and inhibition of dsRNA-activated protein kinase (PKR). Viruses may exploit ADAR1 to suppress antiviral pathways and enhance their replication.
